newsitem.title: SWITZERLAND: U.S. pressed on telecoms pact, WTO boss sees deal.
newsitem.headline: U.S. pressed on telecoms pact, WTO boss sees deal.

text.p: World Trade Organisation chief Renato Ruggiero said on Friday that agreement on a global telecommunications pact seemed within reach, but there were mounting signs that no final decision would come until Saturday.
Major trading powers piled pressure on the United States to agree to what they said was a potentially powerful pact to open up the booming basic telecoms industry to worldwide competition.
"We are not far from a good result, but it is too early to be certain," WTO Director-General Ruggiero told reporters before a meeting of negotiators to assess state of play at the talks.
U.S. Deputy Trade Representative Jeffrey Lang, who has headed Washington's team to the negotiations, marched into the meeting stern-faced and did not stop to talk to reporters.

Trade diplomats said that, despite earlier hopes there may be word from Washington on Friday on whether it would sign up to a deal, there were signs the talks would continue on Saturday with a final meeting before a Geneva deadline of midnight (2300 GMT).
U.S. officials close to WTO talks in Geneva declined all comment on prospects for an accord by the Saturday deadline.

"What is on the table amounts to a massive liberalisation of the world telecommunication market that it would be crazy not to grab with both hands," European Union Trade Commissioner Sir Leon Brittan told a news conference.
"I see no conceivable justification on the basis of what is on the table for failing to clinch the deal," he declared.

A senior negotiator from Canada, which has been strongly targeted by the United States for offering to allow only 46.7 per cent foreign ownership of domestic telecoms companies, said he could not believe the United States would walk away now.
Such action, he said, would ignore "economic and commercial good sense", adding: "I think that at the end of the day, rationality will prevail and we will all sign."
WTO analysts say the long-negotiated pact would cut telephone charges for ordinary users and businesses around the globe and boost markets for new telecoms equipment and services.
In a report, the International Telecommunications Union saw global industry revenues jumping from $800 billion last year to $1.2 trillion at the turn of the century if a deal goes through.
The United States, the world's largest single telecoms market, is vital for a meaningful pact.
Last April, it sank an earlier bid for a pact when it walked away just before a previous deadline saying offers from other countries, primarily emerging economies, were not good enough.
U.S. officials say that to ensure strong public and Congressional backing for a deal at home, it has to be clearly "equitable" with wide enough openings from other countries to match their offer.

Throughout this week, these officials have insisted that improvements in openings currently on the table were needed to finalise a pact. The United States package proposes a full opening of its domestic market to all comers.

Britain, sometimes more attuned to U.S. thinking on economic matters than to that of its EU partners, on Friday joined the chorus of appeals to Washington to line up behind the deal -- which would link a total of 61 countries.
"I would certainly urge the Americans to live up to their rhetoric....and sign up to an accord," Minister for Science and Technology Ian Taylor told a Geneva news conference.

Japanese officials have also said the market opening offers on the table, which include many from small and major emerging economies who did not join the last round of talks, made a good deal and should be sealed in a pact.
Brittan also had an hour-long meeting with Ruggiero, who has called on all countries to make their best efforts for a pact, saying failure could undermine the two-year-old WTO's authority.
